title: WHY DOES THE BIBLE TALK ABOUT BREASTS, KISSING, DESIRE, AND BODIES SO OPENLY?
paragraphs: WHY DOES THE BIBLE TALK ABOUT BREASTS, KISSING, DESIRE, AND BODIES SO OPENLY?
The passages some Christians quietly skip may reveal something beautiful about creation, desire, marriage, shame, holiness—and the God who refuses to abandon our bodies to either lust or disgrace.
There are verses in the Bible that almost nobody volunteers to read aloud in church.
You know the ones.
The verses where lovers kiss.
Where a husband delights in his wife.
Where breasts are mentioned without embarrassment.
Where beauty is noticed.
Where longing is spoken instead of hidden.
Where a man and woman desire one another so intensely that modern Christians sometimes read the passage, look around the room, clear their throats, and quietly move on.
And somewhere along the way, many believers absorbed a strange message:
God is comfortable talking about blood, war, betrayal, murder, crucifixion, demons, judgment, adultery, and death...
but surely He becomes embarrassed when the Bible talks about the human body.
Except He doesn't.
And that should make us ask a question much deeper than whether certain Bible verses make us uncomfortable.
Why did God allow Scripture to speak about kissing, breasts, physical attraction, sexual desire, nakedness, marriage, and bodies so openly?
Maybe because God is not ashamed of what He created.
Maybe because sin did not invent the human body.
Maybe because Satan does not own sexuality.
Maybe because biblical holiness was never supposed to mean pretending desire doesn't exist.
And maybe some of us have spent years trying to make God ashamed of something He originally called good.
Go back before pornography.
Before adultery.
Before exploitation.
Before lust became an industry.
Before human beings learned to use bodies as merchandise.
Before anyone knew what sexual shame felt like.
Genesis says:
"וַיִּבְרָא אֱלֹהִים אֶת־הָאָדָם בְּצַלְמוֹ"
Vayyivra Elohim et-ha'adam betsalmo.
"And God created the human in His image."
Then comes something extraordinary.
Humanity is created male and female, and Genesis 1:31 says God looked upon what He had made and declared it:
"טוֹב מְאֹד"
Tov me'od.
"Very good."
Not barely acceptable.
Not spiritually unfortunate.
Not something God tolerated until human beings could become sufficiently religious to stop having bodies.
Very good.
Then Genesis 2 gives us one of Scripture's most vulnerable descriptions of human existence:
"וַיִּהְיוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם עֲרוּמִּים"
Vayyihyu sheneihem arummim.
"The two of them were naked."
The man and his wife were naked...
and they were not ashamed.
Do not miss that.
Nakedness appears before shame.
The body appears before lust.
Sexual difference appears before sin.
Marriage appears before the Fall.
Human sexuality did not crawl out of humanity's rebellion against God.
It existed within God's good creation.
Then sin entered.
And almost immediately, something happened to the human relationship with the body.
They hid.
That is one of the saddest transitions in the Bible.
Genesis 2 ends with nakedness without shame.
Genesis 3 gives us hiding.
Humanity has been hiding ever since.
We hide our bodies.
We worship our bodies.
We compare our bodies.
We sell bodies.
We exploit bodies.
We obsess over bodies.
We starve bodies.
We abuse bodies.
We use other people's bodies.
We hate our own bodies.
And sometimes religious culture responds to the world's distortion of sexuality by acting as though sexuality itself must have been the problem.
But Scripture refuses that shortcut.
The Bible neither worships sex nor pretends sex does not exist.
It puts desire underneath the lordship of God.
That is why one of the most startling books in Scripture begins with a woman saying:
"יִשָּׁקֵנִי מִנְּשִׁיקוֹת פִּיהוּ"
Yishaqeni minneshiqot pihu.
"Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth."
That is Song of Songs 1:2.
It is in the Bible.
Not hidden in an appendix.
Not smuggled into Scripture by somebody who hoped God wouldn't notice.
There it is.
Desire.
Affection.
Longing.
A kiss.

And Song of Songs becomes even more physically expressive as the poetry unfolds. The lovers admire one another's appearance. They long for one another's presence. They speak of fragrance, touch, beauty, lips, arms, hair, eyes, mouths, and breasts.
Song of Songs 7 even contains the Hebrew:
"שְׁנֵי שָׁדַיִךְ"
Shenei shadayikh.
"Your two breasts."
There is no need to make that phrase dirtier than Scripture makes it.
But there is also no need to pretend it says something else.
The poetry is sensual.
The question is why sensual poetry belongs in Holy Scripture.
And part of the answer may expose two opposite lies our culture keeps telling us.
The first lie says:
"If something is sexual, it must be dirty."
The second says:
"If something is sexual, you should be free to do whatever you desire."
The Bible teaches neither.
Scripture can celebrate marital desire while commanding sexual holiness.
It can acknowledge beauty without turning a person into an object.
It can speak about breasts without becoming pornography.
It can celebrate sexual intimacy without separating intimacy from covenant, faithfulness, responsibility, and love.
That difference matters enormously.
Pornography says, "Take."
Covenant love says, "I give myself faithfully to you."
Pornography separates a body from the dignity of the person inhabiting it.
Biblical love refuses to do that.
Lust asks what another person's body can do for me.
Love asks how I can honor the person God has entrusted to my care.

That is why Proverbs can say to a married man, in remarkably physical language, that he should rejoice in the wife of his youth and be continually delighted by her love. Proverbs 5:19 even speaks openly of her breasts.
Again...
the Bible isn't embarrassed.
But notice the context.
Proverbs 5 is not granting unlimited permission to chase sexual stimulation.
It is doing almost exactly the opposite.
The chapter warns a man against adultery and directs his sexual delight toward his own wife.
Desire is not being erased.
It is being ordered toward faithfulness.
That distinction changes everything.
Christianity does not teach that holiness means becoming less human.
It teaches that everything human—including desire—must be brought under the reign of Jesus Christ.
And Jesus takes desire seriously enough to go beneath behavior and address the heart.
In Matthew 5:28, when Jesus speaks about looking at a woman with lustful intent, the Greek uses a form of:
ἐπιθυμέω
epithymeō.
The word can refer to strong desire or longing; context determines whether that desire is righteous or sinful. Desire itself is therefore not automatically identical with sexual sin.
What Jesus confronts is desire directed toward someone in a way that violates faithfulness in the heart.
He refuses to let us reduce purity to:
"Well, technically, I didn't touch anybody."
Jesus goes after the heart.
The secret stare.
The cultivated fantasy.
The inward possession of another person.
The place nobody sees except you...
and God.
And suddenly this becomes uncomfortable for reasons that have nothing to do with Song of Songs.
Because it is possible to be embarrassed by biblical sexuality while secretly consuming distorted sexuality.
It is possible to blush at the word "breasts" in Scripture and then stare at someone's body online.
It is possible to demand modesty from everybody else while refusing to discipline your own eyes.
It is possible to look sexually respectable in church while carrying an entire hidden world inside your phone.
Maybe that sentence landed somewhere you didn't want it to.
Stay with me.
Because the Gospel is not coming to humiliate you.
It is coming to bring you into the light.
There are people reading this who learned sexuality through pornography before anyone taught them theology.
Some learned it through abuse.
Some through jokes.
Some through shame.
Some through movies.
Some through secret searches at midnight.
Some were told that their body was disgusting.
Some were taught that virtually every sexual feeling was sinful.
Some were never taught anything at all.
And some have spent years trying to figure out whether God is disgusted with them because desire exists inside them.
Listen carefully.
Scripture does not teach that the existence of sexual desire makes you filthy.
It teaches that our desires, like every other dimension of fallen human life, need redemption, wisdom, boundaries, self-control, and surrender to God.
There is a difference between experiencing temptation and choosing to cultivate sin.
There is a difference between noticing beauty and consuming a person with your imagination.
There is a difference between marital delight and exploitation.
There is a difference between intimacy and using someone.
And Christianity's answer to sexual brokenness is not merely:
"Stop wanting."
The Gospel goes deeper.
"Become Christ's."
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 6:19:
And then:
"You are not your own."
Those words are devastating to both sexual shame and sexual entitlement.
To shame, they say:
Your body is not worthless.
To lust, they say:
Neither is anybody else's.
Your body belongs to Christ.
The body you are tempted to hate belongs to Christ.
The body you are tempted to misuse belongs to Christ.
And the person you are tempted to reduce to a body bears a dignity you do not have permission to erase.
Paul's conclusion is magnificent:
"Glorify God in your body."
Not apart from your body.
Not after escaping your body.
In your body.
Christian redemption is astonishingly physical.
Jesus did not merely send us an idea.
ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
Ho Logos sarx egeneto.
"The Word became flesh."
John 1:14.
Flesh.
The eternal Son entered embodied human existence.
He hungered.
He thirsted.
He became tired.
He touched lepers.
He ate meals.
He wept.
He suffered.
He bled.
He died bodily.
And then Christianity makes an even more outrageous claim:
His body did not remain in the grave.
Jesus Christ rose.
Christian hope is not the permanent abandonment of embodiment.
It includes resurrection.
That means the biblical story of the body is bigger than sex.
Creation.
Fall.
Shame.
Incarnation.
Cross.
Resurrection.
Redemption.
Glory.
Your body sits inside that enormous story.

And perhaps that is why Satan has worked so successfully to convince generations of people that their bodies are either gods to worship, products to advertise, weapons to manipulate others, objects to compare, instruments for pleasure, or sources of shame.
Jesus offers another identity.
Redeemed.
Belonging to Him.
This does not make every desire holy.
It means every desire must meet the Holy One.
And some desires must die.
Some habits must be confessed.
Some relationships must change.
Some browser histories need to stop being repeated.
Some secret messages need to end.
Some fantasies need to be starved instead of fed.
Some marriages need tenderness restored.
Some wounded people need time, safety, wise pastoral care, and sometimes professional help because someone else sinned against their body.
Some Christians need to repent of sexual sin.
And some Christians need to repent of making people feel dirty for possessing the ordinary humanity God created them with.
Both errors wound people.
Jesus calls us somewhere better.
Truth without shame.
Grace without compromise.
Holiness without pretending.
Love without exploitation.
Desire without idolatry.
Bodies without worshiping bodies.
Marriage without embarrassment over the intimacy God permits within it.
Singleness without treating unmarried believers as incomplete human beings.
And repentance without believing your scandal gets the final word.
Because maybe this is where the article stops being about "those strange verses in the Bible."
Maybe now it is about you.
About what you watched last night.
About what happened to you years ago.
About the marriage that has become cold.
About the desire you have been hiding.
About the shame you never named.
About the person you keep imagining.
About the addiction everybody thinks you defeated.
About the secret relationship.
About the memory that still makes you feel contaminated.
About the part of your story you are terrified Jesus will uncover.
What if He already knows?
And what if He is still calling you?
The woman caught in adultery had a scandal.
The woman at the well had a complicated relational history.
David had sexual sin in his story.
Corinth contained believers coming out of profoundly broken sexual backgrounds.
The Gospel did not pretend those things were harmless.
Grace never needs to rename darkness as light in order to rescue someone from it.
Jesus does something infinitely better.
He forgives sinners.
He cleanses.
He restores.
He calls people out of darkness.
He teaches them another way to live.
The Christian message is not:
"Your desires determine who you are."
It is:
Jesus Christ can redeem the person your desires could never save.
And perhaps somebody needs that tonight.
You are sitting alone with a screen in your hand.
Nobody knows what you have been fighting.
Nobody knows how many times you promised God it was the last time.
Nobody knows the shame that hits immediately afterward.
Nobody knows how desperately you want to be clean.
You pray.
You fail.
You cry.
You promise.
You relapse.
You hide.
Then Sunday arrives and you know exactly how to smile.
But Jesus knows the person underneath the smile.
He knows what is behind the deleted history.
He knows what happened in that relationship.
He knows what happened to you.
He knows what you willingly chose and what was done to you against your will—and those are not morally the same thing.
He knows where responsibility belongs.
He knows where repentance is needed.
He knows where healing is needed.
And He knows exactly where you are.
The answer is not to run farther into darkness.
Come into the light.
"If we confess our sins, He is faithful and righteous to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
That is 1 John 1:9.
Notice the word cleanse.
Not merely expose.
Cleanse.
This is why the cross matters.
Christianity is not fundamentally a campaign to make sexually broken people behave better.
Christianity announces that the Son of God came for sinners.
At Calvary, Jesus carried sin's judgment.
And when a sinner turns to Christ in repentance and faith, forgiveness is not purchased by performing enough purity afterward.
Christ paid.
Grace is not God's permission to continue living enslaved to sin.
Grace breaks sin's claim to be your master.
Maybe your story contains sexual scandal.
Jesus is not intimidated by scandal.
Maybe your story contains wounds you didn't choose.
Jesus is not frightened by wounds.
Maybe you have spent years believing you are beyond restoration.
Look at the cross again.
There is blood there for sinners.
There is mercy there for the ashamed.
There is a Savior there who knows the entire truth about you and still commands you to come.
Not because sin doesn't matter.
Because He came precisely because it does.
This is why Scripture can speak honestly about bodies.
God intends to redeem whole people.
Your Christianity was never supposed to exist only from the neck upward.
Your eyes belong to Jesus.
Your imagination belongs to Jesus.
Your sexuality belongs to Jesus.
Your singleness belongs to Jesus.
Your marriage belongs to Jesus.
Your wounds belong before Jesus.
Your desires must bow before Jesus.
Your body belongs to Jesus.
And when everything belongs to Him, holiness stops being merely a list of things you aren't allowed to touch.
Holiness becomes freedom to belong completely to the One who died and rose for you.
So yes.
The Bible talks about kissing.
It talks about breasts.
It talks about desire.
It talks about nakedness.
It talks about sex.
It talks about adultery.
It talks about lust.
It talks about marriage.
It talks about bodies.
And it does so because the God of Scripture is not afraid of the truth about being human.
He created what sin distorted.
He confronts what lust corrupts.
He protects what exploitation cheapens.
He forgives what repentance brings into the light.
And through Jesus Christ, He is restoring what the Fall shattered.
Be honest.

And if your story is too personal to explain publicly, you don't owe strangers your private details. Even a simple "no more hiding" can become your reminder that darkness does not get to own the rest of your story.
Not because clicking "Share" earns favor with God. It doesn't.
It cannot.
Salvation is grace.
Someone's marriage may be hurting.
Someone may think pornography has permanently disqualified them from Christ.
Someone may have confused holiness with hatred of their own body.
Someone may desperately need to discover that repentance is not the doorway to rejection.
It is the road home to grace.
Send it to the believer who has been fighting silently.
The Gospel cannot be bought. Give freely, prayerfully, and without compulsion.
Surrender to Jesus.
If there is sin, repent.
If there is shame, bring it into His light.
If you have fallen, stop running away from the only Savior capable of raising you.
If you have been wounded, know that what someone did to you does not make you morally dirty.
If you are married, honor your covenant.
If you are single, do not believe the lie that sexual experience is required for a meaningful human life. Jesus Himself lived a fully human life without marriage or sexual intercourse.
If desire is raging, don't worship it and don't pretend it isn't there.
Bring it under Christ.
Because Christianity does not end with a frightened sinner hiding behind leaves.
It ends with redeemed people belonging completely to God.
That is the journey.
From nakedness without shame...
to sin and hiding...
to bodies distorted by lust and wounded by exploitation...
to the Word becoming flesh...
to a Savior's body broken on a cross...
to an empty tomb...
to resurrection...
to redemption...
to glory.
So the next time someone asks:
"Why does the Bible talk about breasts, kissing, desire, and bodies so openly?"
Tell them:
Because God is not embarrassed by His creation.
Because He tells the truth about our corruption of it.
Because holiness does not require pretending we have no bodies.
Because desire needs redemption, not worship.
Because sex is not God.
Because shame is not God either.
Because our bodies were never meant to belong to lust, pornography, exploitation, culture, comparison, or ourselves.
They were meant to glorify the One who created them.

And because when sin turned nakedness into hiding, God began unfolding a redemption story that would eventually lead to Jesus Christ—the Savior who entered human flesh, carried human sin, died a human death, walked bodily out of a grave, and now calls ashamed sinners out from behind whatever they have been hiding behind.
Maybe that is why this subject makes us uncomfortable.
It gets too close.
Too close to our browser histories.
Too close to our marriages.
Too close to our wounds.
Too close to our fantasies.
Too close to our shame.
Too close to the places where we desperately want Jesus...
but still haven't completely opened the door.
Open it.
He already knows what is behind it.
And grace is standing closer than your shame wants you to believe.
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your story, but only Jesus gets to write the ending.
